title: Teaching Problem Solving (Kind Of)
author: Latimir, Craig
summary: Craig Latimir, drawing on a MathsConf talk, argues that exam-board "problem solving" (AO3) questions are narrower and more predictable than the term suggests, which is good news because it means the underlying skills can be explicitly taught rather than left to develop only in naturally strong students. He proposes closing the resulting attainment gap by distilling and directly teaching the implicit strategies that already-successful problem-solvers use without realising it. His two named strategies are "number-free problems," where students are trained to ignore the numbers in a question on first read and instead build a plan using only its underlying structure before any calculation begins, and "zoom-in zoom-out," where students learn to mentally isolate just the relevant portion of a complex geometric diagram rather than being overwhelmed by the whole figure. He grounds "number-free problems" in working-memory limits, arguing that attending to numeric detail too early crowds out the capacity needed to grasp a problem's underlying structure. He closes by insisting these strategies must be interleaved throughout the curriculum and referred to repeatedly from an early stage, rather than introduced as an isolated unit near exams.
points: Latimir's reframe of AO3 "problem solving" as narrower and more predictable than it sounds is the argument's hinge: if the skill set is bounded, it's teachable, which is the basis for his equity claim about closing the attainment gap.

His "number-free problems" strategy is explicitly grounded in working-memory theory, ignoring numeric detail on first read frees capacity to engage with a problem's deep structure rather than its surface features.

"Zoom-in zoom-out" targets a specific failure mode in geometry problems: students overwhelmed by a full diagram rather than mentally isolating the two or three elements actually needed to solve for an unknown.
He explicitly rejects treating problem-solving strategies as a one-off unit, arguing they need interleaving and repeated reference across a student's full schooling to become genuinely internalised.
quotes: These do not, however, represent the sort of problem solving students need to perform well in a KS2-KS5 terminal exam.
It shows that the types of questions that assess a student’s ability to problem solve can be quite narrow and predictable. Because of that, it makes the skills needed to succeed with them teachable.
The human brain can hold about 7 things in its working memory at any one time. If you focus on the surface details, in this case the numbers, then you are taking up valuable space.
My argument is that those students who successfully answer questions like this are already doing this strategy. We just need to make the implicit explicit.
This involves distilling the things that experts do implicitly, automatically, and turning them into named strategies that are embedded throughout a curriculum.
